title: Compact SDK Onramp: smoke tests, gating & sample-app flows (draft)
body:
Context:
This is a compact, opinionated onramp playbook for the SDK surface we want new engineering users (internal and external) to complete in their first 20–60 minutes. The idea: reduce cognitive load, provide a tiny deterministic success loop (install -> auth -> first request -> local smoke tests -> sample app run), and protect master/main with lightweight CI gating so we don't ship regressions in the tiny demo flows that customers rely on when onboarding.

Goals (what success looks like):
- Developer can go from zero to first successful generation in < 10 minutes using either the JS or Python SDK.
- Local smoke tests provide deterministic checks (auth, basic request, streaming path, error backoff) that run in CI on PRs touching SDK or sample apps.
- Sample app (single-page web + simple server) starts locally and mirrors a minimal production pattern: auth via env var, request + stream, render partial tokens, handle errors and retry.
- CI gating: PRs that touch SDK core or sample apps must pass the smoke-suite; flaky tests are tracked and triaged within 48h.
- Telemetry: onboarding success/failure points instrumented so we can measure drop-off (install, auth, first request, streaming).

Audience:
- External customers evaluating Redwood-hosted API who try the SDK quickstart.
- Internal new hires (SEs, Solutions, SDK maintainers) who need a consistent way to validate local installs.

Non-goals:
- Full E2E QA for every model variant. This is intentionally minimal and orthogonal to our production test matrix.

Core components (minimal set):
1) Quickstart README (two pages):
   - Page A: install + env var auth + 3-line request example (JS + Py). Keep code visible first, explanation below.
   - Page B: run sample app locally, what to expect, common errors and fixes (port conflicts, CORS, auth errors).

2) Smoke-suite (single-file runnable):
   - Runs headless: uses local env creds or CI token.
   - Checks: auth (401/403 handling), basic generation (short prompt -> deterministic-ish output pattern check), streaming path (connect + receive first token within Xms), embedding call (sanity), and error-handling path (simulate rate limit -> confirm retry/backoff logic).
   - Exit codes: 0 = pass, non-0 = fail with structured output for CI logs.

3) Sample app (starter):
   - Minimal SPA (React/Vite) + Node/Flask server that proxies allowing secret-free frontend demos in local mode using env var token on server.
   - Features: streaming render with incremental updates, abort button, simple retry UI, token usage meter stub, and a tiny transcription to show streaming stability.

4) CI gating jobs:
   - smoke-on-pr: run smoke-suite on Node + Py matrix for PRs touching src/, examples/, and docs/quickstart.md.
   - smoke-nightly: run full smoke-suite + sample-app headless runner against canonical hosted endpoint every night.
   - Fail fast policy: PRs must fix failures before merge; flaky tests get ticketed automatically.

Developer experience flows (happy path):
1) Install: npm i @redwood/inference / pip install redwood-inference
2) Export API key: export REDWOOD_API_KEY=sk-xxx
3) Run minimal example: node quickstart.js or python quickstart.py -> prints streaming tokens and final `OK`
4) Run smoke locally: npm run smoke or python -m redwood.smoke -> returns `PASS`
5) Clone sample app and run: cd examples/simple-chat && npm run dev -> open http://localhost:3000, interact, observe streaming and retry behavior

Local smoke-suite design notes (quick):
- Keep it deterministic: use short hard-coded prompts and assert on presence of keywords rather than full text equality. Example: prompt = "Summarize: apples vs bananas" -> assert response contains "apples" and "bananas".
- Timeouts: streaming first-token threshold = 2s in CI; full generation timeout = 8s for the smoke suite.
- Backoff simulation: client sends a request with header `X-Sim-429: 1` to trigger deterministic 429 from our test harness (server stub or sandbox model). Assert that client waits then retries at least once.
- Network isolation for CI: smoke runs must be hermetic for non-hosted paths. When calling hosted API, use a stable test token with low rate limits to avoid flakiness.

Sample-app acceptance checklist (local):
- [ ] App starts and serves static bundle on expected port.
- [ ] Token is read from env var and not hard-coded in frontend.
- [ ] Streaming shows partial tokens and final result.
- [ ] Abort button cancels request and UI returns to idle.
- [ ] Retry recovers from simulated 429.
- [ ] Minimal telemetry events emitted (onboard.start, onboard.first_request, onboard.success, onboard.error) logged to console in dev mode.

CI implementation considerations:
- Use a dedicated low-priv test key scoped to smoke endpoints. Rotate monthly.
- Secret management: store token in GH Actions secrets / CircleCI; restrict PR-level usage to forks via ephemeral tokens.
- Runners: Linux x86 matrix plus macOS for JS dev flow parity. Python tests run on multiple minor versions (3.10, 3.11).

Telemetry plan (quick):
- Emit lightweight events from the quickstart script and sample app dev server. Events should include step id, success/fail, duration (ms), SDK version. Send to internal ingestion only.
- Dashboard tickets: raw funnel (install -> auth -> first_request -> smoke_pass). Goal: baseline 70% success for first-time external users; if < 50% escalate to DX team.

Open questions / decisions to make:
- Do we enforce PR gating on docs changes that touch quickstart snippets? (Pro: prevents rot. Con: slows content edits.) Proposal: only gate if code snippets are runnable via smoke-suite; docs-only edits should still run a lightweight snippet-linter in CI.
- How to handle model nondeterminism in streaming assertions? Current plan: assert token presence or regex patterns, not full equality. Need an approval from Applied ML on acceptable fingerprinting checks.
- Flaky-test policy: define threshold (3 occurrences in 7 days) to flip flaky -> quarantine. Who owns triage? Suggest devx on-call with rotating rotation.

Roadmap (next 8 weeks):
- Week 1: consolidate quickstart README + minimal examples (Aisha)
- Week 2: implement smoke-suite Node + Py; basic CI job (Liam)
- Week 3: sample-app skeleton + streaming UX (Marcos)
- Week 4: instrument telemetry + dashboard stub (Nicole)
- Week 5: integrate CI gating and secret provisioning; docs lint job for snippet verification
- Week 6: dogfood: run new quickstart with solutions team and record friction points; iterate
- Week 7: address flaky failures and finalize gating policy; draft rollout notes
- Week 8: public beta publish and measure funnel for two weeks

Quick checklist for reviewers:
- Do the smoke checks cover critical onboarding failure modes? (auth, streaming, basic generation, backoff)
- Are the acceptance checks too strict given model variance? (ok to relax to keyword assertions)
- CI cost estimate: are nightly smoke runs acceptable? (approx 1h of runner time)
- Telemetry: do we have PII risk? only send metrics & hashed ids.

Notes / scratch ideas (short):
- Consider a CLI flag `--fast-onramp` that runs an ultra-light subset for demo environments.
- Add a `redwood dev proxy` dev tool to simplify CORS/proxy issues with frontend demos.
- Keep sample-app UI intentionally ugly but functional; focus on observable behaviors (stream, abort, retry).

Unresolved TODOs (owner tagged):
- [Aisha] Draft quickstart minimal README and examples.
- [Liam] Prototype smoke-suite in Node and Py and add CI job stub.
- [Marcos] Build sample-app skeleton with streaming demo and retry UI.
- [Nicole] Instrument telemetry & create Confluence dashboard page.

Bottom line: This playbook aims to give every new dev a tiny, repeatable success loop and a CI safety net so that onboarding examples remain trustworthy. Feedback wanted on the smoke-suite assertions and the gating scope.
